title: Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation for Promoting Recovery of Consciousness in Patients With Early Disorders of Consciousness: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
summary: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the potential short-term therapeutic effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) on the recovery of consciousness in ...
fullText:
Journal: Brain And Behavior • PMID: 43099981

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the potential short-term therapeutic effect of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) on the recovery of consciousness in patients with early disorders of consciousness (DOC).

METHODS: A total of 60 patients with early DOC were randomly assigned, and 57 completed the primary outcome assessment and were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The intervention group received 10 Hz tACS targeting the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), whereas the control group received sham stimulation. Participants in both groups continued to receive conventional rehabilitation therapy. Neurobehavioral and electrophysiological assessments were conducted at baseline and after 14 days of intervention using the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R), the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), electroencephalography (EEG), and mismatch negativity (MMN).

RESULTS: For the primary outcome, the CRS-R score was significantly higher in the intervention group than in the control group (F = 4.187, p = 0.046, partial η2 = 0.072). Sensitivity analysis yielded findings consistent with the primary analysis (Z = -2.042, p = 0.041). Improvement in GCS score was also significantly greater in the intervention group compared with the control group (Z = -2.637, p = 0.008). Neuroelectrophysiological findings indicated a significantly greater improvement in MMN elicitation in the intervention group relative to the control group (Z = -2.111, p = 0.035). Although EEG grading demonstrated a trend toward improvement, no statistically significant difference between the groups was identified (Z = -1.329, p = 0.184).

CONCLUSION: When combined with conventional rehabilitation, a 2-week course of 10 Hz tACS applied to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was associated with short-term, baseline-adjusted improvements in recovery of consciousness and behavioral responses in patients with early DOC. These preliminary findings suggest that 10 Hz tACS targeting the DLPFC may represent a potential adjunctive strategy for facilitating consciousness recovery in early DOC.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN registration number: ISRCTN15236545.

title: Treatment outcomes among obese and non-obese women at high-risk of gestational diabetes: secondary analysis of the CDC4G clinical trial.
summary: BACKGROUND: We examined whether the association between treatment and adverse pregnancy outcomes among high-risk women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) differed by mat...
fullText:
Journal: Bmc Medicine • PMID: 43099518

BACKGROUND: We examined whether the association between treatment and adverse pregnancy outcomes among high-risk women with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) differed by maternal obesity status.

METHODS: We conducted a secondary analysis of The Changing Diagnostic Criteria for Gestational Diabetes (CDC4G) trial, a prospective, unblinded, stepped-wedge cluster randomised clinical trial evaluating the implementation of the WHO-2013 GDM diagnostic criteria among women screened based on risk factors. The trial was conducted in 2018 with follow-up to August 2019. We included women whose GDM diagnosis based on a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test was discordant between the Swedish-GDM criteria (fasting plasma glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L and/or a region-specific 2-hour plasma glucose threshold ranging from 8.9 to < 11.1 mmol/L) and the modified WHO-2013 criteria (fasting plasma glucose ≥ 5.1 mmol/L and/or 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ 8.5 mmol/L). The 1-hour plasma glucose criterion could not be evaluated because these measurements were unavailable before implementation of the WHO-2013 criteria. Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m² and non-obesity as BMI 18.5-29.9 kg/m². The primary outcome was large-for-gestational-age neonate (LGA), defined as birthweight > 90th percentile by Swedish reference standards. Multilevel Poisson and multinomial regression models adjusted for baseline characteristics were used.

RESULTS: Among 2069 women with discordant classification by diagnostic criteria, 917 (55.9% with obesity) were undiagnosed and untreated, and 1152 (46.3% with obesity) were diagnosed and treated. In multivariable models, treatment did not reduce the risk of LGA among women with obesity (relative risk (RR) 0.94, 95% CI 0.81-1.08) but reduced risk among women without obesity (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.54-0.88), interaction P < .01.

CONCLUSIONS: Among high-risk women, implementing the WHO-2013 GDM diagnostic criteria was associated with a reduced risk of LGA among women without obesity, but not among women with obesity, partly reflecting the baseline lower risk of LGA among treated women with obesity than untreated women without obesity. Interpretation is limited by the absence of data on glycaemic control during pregnancy. Further research should evaluate how maternal characteristics modify treatment effectiveness to optimise management strategies for women with GDM.

title: Liver resection, transplantation, and local therapies for hepatocellular carcinoma: a Brazilian multidisciplinary consensus.
summary: BACKGROUND: Curative treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma is limited to strategies that achieve complete tumor eradication, primarily liver resection, liver transplantation,...
fullText:
Journal: Arquivos Brasileiros De Cirurgia Digestiva : Abcd = Brazilian Archives Of Digestive Surgery • PMID: 43097550

BACKGROUND: Curative treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma is limited to strategies that achieve complete tumor eradication, primarily liver resection, liver transplantation, and locoregional therapies. However, therapeutic decision-making is complex and must balance tumor burden, liver function, patient characteristics, and resource availability.

AIMS: To develop multidisciplinary, evidence-based recommendations for the use of surgical and locoregional therapies in hepatocellular carcinoma management.

METHODS: The Brazilian Society of Surgical Oncology coordinated this consensus in collaboration with 13 additional Brazilian medical societies. A scientific steering committee identified clinically relevant questions addressing indications, patient selection, technical considerations, and outcomes related to liver resection, liver transplantation, and locoregional therapies.

RESULTS: A total of 36 clinical questions reached consensus, generating evidence-based recommendations across three major domains: liver resection, including criteria for resectability, assessment of liver functional reserve, and strategies to expand surgical candidacy; liver transplantation, addressing selection criteria, expanded eligibility concepts, donor source considerations, and the role of bridging and downstaging therapies; and locoregional therapies, encompassing ablative and intra-arterial treatments, their indications as definitive, bridging, or alternative strategies, and their integration within multidisciplinary care pathways.

CONCLUSIONS: This multidisciplinary consensus provides structured, evidence-based guidance on the use of liver resection, liver transplantation, and locoregional therapies in hepatocellular carcinoma management. By addressing key clinical questions about patient selection, therapeutic indications, and integration of curative and locoregional strategies, these recommendations aim to support consistent, informed decision-making in daily clinical practice and to optimize outcomes for patients eligible for potentially curative treatment.

RACIONAL:: O tratamento curativo do carcinoma hepatocelular (CHC) limita-se a estratégias que visam à erradicação completa do tumor, principalmente a ressecção hepática, o transplante hepático e as terapias locorregionais. No entanto, a tomada de decisão terapêutica é complexa e deve equilibrar a carga tumoral, a função hepática, as características do paciente e a disponibilidade de recursos.

OBJETIVOS:: Desenvolver recomendações multidisciplinares, baseadas em evidências, para o uso de terapias cirúrgicas e locorregionais no manejo do CHC.

MÉTODOS:: Este consenso foi coordenado pela Sociedade Brasileira de Cirurgia Oncológica em colaboração com outras 13 sociedades médicas brasileiras. Um comitê científico diretivo identificou questões clinicamente relevantes, abrangendo indicações, seleção de pacientes, considerações técnicas e desfechos relacionados à ressecção hepática, ao transplante hepático e às terapias locorregionais.

RESULTADOS:: Um total de 36 questões clínicas alcançaram consenso, gerando recomendações baseadas em evidências em três domínios principais: ressecção hepática, incluindo critérios de ressecabilidade, avaliação da reserva funcional hepática e estratégias para ampliar a elegibilidade cirúrgica; transplante hepático, abordando critérios de seleção, conceitos de elegibilidade expandidos, considerações sobre a fonte do doador e o papel das terapias de ponte; e terapias locorregionais, abrangendo tratamentos ablativos e intra-arteriais, suas indicações como estratégias definitivas, de ponte ou alternativas e sua integração em vias de atendimento multidisciplinares.

CONCLUSÕES:: Este consenso multidisciplinar fornece orientações estruturadas e baseadas em evidências sobre o uso de ressecção hepática, transplante hepático e terapias locorregionais no tratamento do CHC. Ao abordar questões clínicas importantes relacionadas à seleção de pacientes, indicações terapêuticas e integração de estratégias curativas e locorregionais, essas recomendações visam apoiar a tomada de decisões consistentes e informadas na prática clínica diária e otimizar os resultados para pacientes elegíveis para tratamento potencialmente curativo.

title: Adjunctive ursodeoxycholic acid in type 2 diabetes: a randomized controlled open-label pilot study.
summary: PURPOSE: Adequate glycemic control remains difficult to achieve. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has shown potential glycemic benefits in chronic liver disease patients and anti-i...
fullText:
Journal: Endocrine • PMID: 43097300

PURPOSE: Adequate glycemic control remains difficult to achieve. Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has shown potential glycemic benefits in chronic liver disease patients and anti-inflammatory effects in animal models of type 2 diabetes. This pilot study investigated the effect of UDCA as adjunctive therapy on metabolic and inflammatory biomarkers in patients with type 2 diabetes.

METHODS: Patients were randomized to control and UDCA groups. All patients received metformin 1000 mg plus vildagliptin 50 mg twice daily. The UDCA group received additional UDCA 450 mg twice daily. Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included fasting blood glucose (FBG), lipid profile, body mass index (BMI), C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), high mobility group box 1 (HMGB-1), asprosin, malondialdehyde (MDA), and A-kinase anchoring protein 1 (AKAP1). Outcomes were assessed at baseline and after three months.

RESULTS: Per-protocol analysis included forty-four patients per group. After three months, the UDCA group had significantly lower HbA1c (P = 0.001) than the control group. Among secondary outcomes, only IL-6 remained significantly lower in the UDCA group than in the control group after adjusting for multiple comparisons (P < 0.001, q = 0.017). Other secondary biomarkers did not differ significantly between groups. Biomarker findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

CONCLUSION: Adjunctive UDCA was associated with a possible improvement in glycemic control, while biomarker changes should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. However, per‑protocol analysis may overestimate treatment effects, and the open‑label design and predominantly female cohort limit generalizability. These findings require confirmation in larger, intention‑to‑treat trials.

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: This trial​ was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov under identifiers NCT05902468 (registration date: 15-6-2023).

title: New WHO technical package to help countries improve health data for COVID-19 response and beyond
summary: Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new a...
fullText:
Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many countries still lack both the infrastructure to routinely gather health data and the analytical capacity to use these data for effective health actions and emergency response. “Countries must be able to measure progress to make progress,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Particularly during COVID-19, reliable data is the best way to coordinate response efforts and improve health in all areas.” Accurate health data are necessary to understand specific country needs in order to improve health and save lives. Data also helps direct scarce resources to where they are needed most. The SCORE (Survey, Count, Optimize, Review, Enable) Technical Package aims to improve the availability of timely, reliable, validated, and comparable health data. For the first time in a single, harmonized package, it represents all the key elements for optimized health information system performance. Simply put, SCORE will help governments around the globe set benchmarks and improve standards in healthcare.In response to the challenges of data availability highlighted in the WHO World Health Statistics 2020 report, SCORE includes more than 90 universally-accepted tools and standards for health information systems strengthening. “Using data to inform public health priorities and strategies has never been more important,” said Dr Kelly Henning, Director of Public Health Programs at Bloomberg Philanthropies[2]. “The SCORE Technical Package provides country governments around the world with high-quality, essential technical guidance so that countries can strengthen their own data systems.” WHO is proud to partner with the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative to deliver this timely resource to countries.  Below are some examples of how SCORE can improve individual lives and communities:The birth of a child is registered so they can access essential health services, attend school, and apply for a passport;A death is registered with cause-of-death accurately captured so that policy-makers have a better understanding of all-cause and COVID-specific mortality and associated risk factors and implement programs and policies to save lives;Health data are disaggregated by age, sex and cause of death to illustrate the root causes of health disparities and help direct resources to the most vulnerable groups such as those who do not speak the local language or face stigma and discrimination in their community; Health facilities have the capacity to regularly measure the quality of their services, workforce and patient data and can make a compelling case for increased funding to national and international stakeholders;Health data are integrated with other sectors so that social determinants of health such as pollution, sanitation and nutrition are addressed to reduce the overall burden of disease.The package's initial release includes two documents: SCORE Essential Interventions – including an overview of health information systems, underlying elements, and indicators to assess progress with sample actions; andSCORE Tools and Standards -- including resources to address critical health data gaps and strengthen country health data.“We must keep score to save lives. WHO is committed to working with countries and partners to rapidly scale up capacity for data collection and use in order to improve policy and performance,” added Dr Samira Asma, Assistant Director-General for Data, Analytics and Delivery for Impact at WHO. “We must act now to invest in statistical systems in countries, respond to this pandemic and meet the SDGs and the Triple Billion targets. Our window of opportunity is closing, and we cannot wait to address data gaps. Data use to address country needs has to be a priority today.”Country-owned, disaggregated data will be essential for more resilient and sustainable health systems going forward. COVID-19 is both a wake-up call and a stark reminder of the challenges we still have to address. But it is also an opportunity to build back better through solidarity, information-sharing and collaboration. SCORE is one example of how a collaborative approach can benefit countries by providing a common set of tools based on shared standards. This package is designed to be practical, actionable and flexible. We will only be successful in combatting COVID-19 if we work together.Future components of the SCORE Technical Package are due to be released later this year, including the SCORE Assessment Instrument and global, regional and country status reports.  Together, these will provide a complete package of information to plan and monitor progress against national and subnational priorities as well as global targets.-----[1] https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do/thirteenth-general-programme-of-work-2019---2023#:~:text=The%20Thirteenth%20General%20Programme%20of,health%20at%20the%20country%20leve[2] Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative provided funding to support the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package

title: COVID-19 disrupting mental health services in most countries, WHO survey
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted or halted critical mental health services in 93% of countries worldwide while the demand for mental health is increasing, according to a ne...
fullText:
The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted or halted critical mental health services in 93% of countries worldwide while the demand for mental health is increasing, according to a new WHO survey. The survey of 130 countries provides the first global data showing the devastating impact of COVID-19 on access to mental health services and underscores the urgent need for increased funding.The survey was published ahead of WHO’s Big Event for Mental Health  ̶  a global online advocacy event on 10 October that will bring together world leaders, celebrities, and advocates to call for increased mental health investments in the wake of COVID-19.WHO has previously highlighted the chronic underfunding of mental health: prior to the pandemic, countries were spending less than 2 per cent of their national health budgets on mental health, and struggling to meet their populations’ needs.And the pandemic is increasing demand for mental health services. Bereavement, isolation, loss of income and fear are triggering mental health conditions or exacerbating existing ones. Many people may be facing increased levels of alcohol and drug use, insomnia, and anxiety. Meanwhile, COVID-19 itself can lead to neurological and mental complications, such as delirium, agitation, and stroke. People with pre-existing mental, neurological or substance use disorders are also more vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection  ̶  they may stand a higher risk of severe outcomes and even death. “Good mental health is absolutely fundamental to overall health and well-being,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “COVID-19 has interrupted essential mental health services around the world just when they’re needed most. World leaders must move fast and decisively to invest more in life-saving mental health programmes  ̶  during the pandemic and beyond.”  Survey finds major disruptions to critical mental health services The survey was conducted from June to August 2020 among 130 countries across WHO’s six regions. It evaluates how the provision of mental, neurological and substance use services has changed due to COVID-19, the types of services that have been disrupted, and how countries are adapting to overcome these challenges.Countries reported widespread disruption of many kinds of critical mental health services:Over 60% reported disruptions to mental health services for vulnerable people, including children and adolescents (72%), older adults (70%), and women requiring antenatal or postnatal services (61%).67% saw disruptions to counseling and psychotherapy; 65% to critical harm reduction services; and 45% to opioid agonist maintenance treatment for opioid dependence.More than a third (35%) reported disruptions to emergency interventions, including those for people experiencing prolonged seizures; severe substance use withdrawal syndromes; and delirium, often a sign of a serious underlying medical condition.30% reported disruptions to access for medications for mental, neurological and substance use disorders. Around three-quarters reported at least partial disruptions to school and workplace mental health services (78% and 75% respectively). While many countries (70%) have adopted telemedicine or teletherapy to overcome disruptions to in-person services, there are significant disparities in the uptake of these interventions. More than 80% of high-income countries reported deploying telemedicine and teletherapy to bridge gaps in mental health, compared with less than 50% of low-income countries. WHO has issued guidance to countries on how to maintain essential services  ̶  including mental health services  ̶  during COVID-19 and recommends that countries allocate resources to mental health as an integral component of their response and recovery plans. The Organization also urges countries to monitor changes and disruptions in services so that they can address them as required.Although 89% of countries reported in the survey that mental health and psychosocial support is part of their national COVID-19 response plans, only 17% of these countries have full additional funding for covering these activities.This all highlights the need for more money for mental health. As the pandemic continues, even greater demand will be placed on national and international mental health programmes that have suffered from years of chronic underfunding. Spending 2% of national health budgets on mental health is not enough. International funders also need to do more: mental health still receives less than 1% of international aid earmarked for health.Those who do invest in mental health will reap rewards. Pre-COVID-19 estimates reveal that nearly US$ 1 trillion in economic productivity is lost annually from depression and anxiety alone. However, studies show that every US$ 1 spent on evidence-based care for depression and anxiety returns US$5. Note on World Mental Health Day: Mobilizing the global community to #MoveforMentalHeatlh On World Mental Health Day (Saturday 10 October), as part of its campaign Move for mental health: let’s invest, WHO is inviting the global community to take part in The Big Event for Mental Health, an unprecedented online advocacy event that will call for increased investment in mental health at all levels  ̶  from individuals to businesses to countries to civil society  ̶  so that the world can begin to close the gaps highlighted by today’s report. The Big Event is free and open to the public and will be broadcast on 10 October from 16:00 to 19:00 CEST on WHO’s YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, TikTok and LinkedIn channels and website. For updated information about the Big Event for Mental Health, including the latest lineup of performances and participants, visit the Big Event web page. To learn more about World Mental Health Day, visit WHO’s campaign page.
